What differs in AI by industry, and what stays the same in every sector?

In AI by industry, the questions are the same in every sector: deciding which applications get priority, choosing a vendor or build partner, and keeping the application in hand after go-live. The differences sit in the rules, the sensitivity of the data, and the cost of error, and those decide how heavily each step gets weighted.
When do the rules for high-risk applications apply in AI by industry?

From 2 December 2027, the rules for high-risk applications apply following the Digital Omnibus, and from 2 August 2028 for AI in products such as medical devices; those rules have been postponed. In AI by industry, the AI Act lays a layer over sector rules, with obligations that vary by application.
Are there case studies for every sector in AI by industry?

No. There are case studies from financial services, retail, manufacturing and professional services in the cases overview. For healthcare, marketing, automotive, education, aviation and the public sector, the AI by industry pages describe the questions and rules, not results of their own.

Updated: October 2026.

Look at AI by industry and the differences stand out first: a hospital has different processes to a bank, a marketing team works with different data to a local authority. Even so, the underlying questions look remarkably alike. Someone has to decide which applications get priority, which vendor or build partner fits, and how you stay in control once it’s live. Prioritise, choose, embed: that’s the work, in every sector.
Sector knowledge matters in three places:

Rules. Healthcare has medical-device regulation, financial services has its own regulators, the public sector has rules on decisions that affect citizens. The AI Act lays a further layer on top, with obligations that vary by application.
Data. Health data, financial transactions and customer profiles each demand different handling. What’s an ordinary dataset in one sector is a special category of personal data in another.
Cost of error. A badly generated product description is annoying. A wrong credit decision or triage call is a different order of problem. How much human oversight you build in depends on that.
PrioritiseWhich applications pay off and are achievable? The same in every sector.
ChooseBuy, build or partner: the same trade-off, different requirements.
EmbedOwnership, measurement and adjustment after go-live.
Sector layerRules, data sensitivity and the cost of error set how strict each step needs to be.
The approach is the same everywhere; the sector decides how heavily you weight each step.

A note on my own background: my work leans most heavily on financial services, retail, manufacturing and professional services. For other sectors I bring the approach; sector-specific questions also need someone who knows the domain from the inside.
A leasing company with 140 staff wants to use AI to process private-lease applications faster. The original plan: a model that pre-assesses every application and gives an approval recommendation.

The adviser tests the plan from the client's side. Advice on an individual's creditworthiness falls into the AI Act's high-risk category, with requirements from 2 December 2027. The team splits the question accordingly: AI extracts data from payslips and bank statements, the underwriter keeps making the assessment. The extraction comes from a vendor the leasing company contracts directly.

Outcome: across roughly 1,100 applications a month, retyping falls from 20 to 8 minutes per application, around 220 hours a month combined. An automatic approval recommendation deliberately isn't introduced, as long as there's no plan for the high-risk requirements.
Fictional example, built from situations that come up often. The organisation and figures are illustrative.
For financial services and automotive, I’ve built a dedicated page with the key applications, the rules that come into play and the pitfalls that tend to recur.

Banks, insurers and fintechs work under heavy supervision. Credit scoring of individuals, and risk assessment and pricing for life and health insurance, count as high-risk under the AI Act. How to handle that responsibly is covered in AI in fintech and financial services.

In the automotive chain, AI touches everything from sales and the workshop to customer contact. Many of the questions overlap with the broader manufacturing sector. More on the page about AI in automotive.

Other sectors, including healthcare, marketing, education, aviation and the public sector, each carry their own rules and data sensitivities, and more sector pages are planned. If your sector isn’t covered yet, AI for business is a better starting point, and what the AI Act asks per application is covered on the AI policy page. Note that the rules for high-risk applications have been postponed: since the Digital Omnibus they apply from 2 December 2027, and for AI in products such as medical devices from 2 August 2028 (European Commission).
Most of the case studies on this site come from the sectors my work leans on most heavily. They show how the same approach plays out in a different context:
Financial services: a KYC process with AI-supported document analysis, where the analyst always keeps the final check, and a use-case portfolio for an investment firm.
Retail: a structured vendor selection in enterprise retail, where the criteria were fixed before any vendor came to the table.
Manufacturing: an AI roadmap for a global manufacturer, bringing scattered pilots under one governance structure.
Professional services: an internal AI assistant for knowledge workers, where adoption took more work than the technology.
For healthcare, marketing, automotive, education, aviation and the public sector, there are no case studies on the site yet. All case studies are in the cases overview.
